mainEntity.name: Can I change the content myself after handover?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, that's the point. The content model and handover document list every section you're meant to update, and exactly where you change it.

mainEntity.name: Who owns the code and domain?

acceptedAnswer.text: You do. Source code, domain and hosting account, all handed over in your name.

mainEntity.name: Do you redesign our current site or start from scratch?

acceptedAnswer.text: Either works. During Discover we look at what's worth keeping from the current site, and the scope says what we decided.

mainEntity.name: Which content management system do you use?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on who'll be changing content, and how often. Whatever we pick, the choice and the reason go into the scope.

Website building

Someone messages your shop at midnight, ready to buy. By morning that message sits under fifty newer ones, and the sale's gone. A website doesn't bury orders and doesn't need you online. We build you one, with price and deliverables settled on paper before work starts.
Why orders get lost

Most people who come to us are stuck in one of two spots. Either their site can only be touched by whoever built it, so a one-line change means waiting, and paying again. Or they're getting a different price from everyone they ask, with no clear picture of what they'd actually receive.
It plays out the same way. A month becomes three. Every week brings one more "just add this." At the end, nobody can say what the final price is, or who's responsible for what.

We're Roxana Negaresh and Arshia Amani, and we've watched that film too many times. So we don't start without a written scope: what's being built, what it costs, when it lands, all on paper first. The code and domain are yours, the handover document comes with the site, and after launch you change content yourself. We've also written up what a website price is actually made of, and if you sell on Instagram, why an Instagram shop needs a website of its own.
This is for you if

items: You're building your first serious site and want to update it yourself afterwards, without calling anyone.
Your current site is slow, or only its previous builder dares touch it.
You need Persian and English versions that both work properly, not one good one and one afterthought.

blocks.html: Honestly, skip us if

items: A ready-made template in your colours would do the job. A site builder does that for less money.
You need to be online within days. There isn't time to scope it properly, and we won't skip that step.
You want building to start before any content exists, with the words arriving "later", and you don't want that risk written into the scope.

blocks.html: How a build runs

items: Discover. Input: talking with you, plus any content that already exists. Output: a brief and a draft scope. Owner: dadmor, with your answers.
Model. Input: the brief. Output: the site map and a content model, meaning which sections each page has and who updates them. Owner: dadmor; approval: you.
Design. Input: the site map you approved. Output: a design system and the key pages. Owner: dadmor; feedback: you.
Build. Input: the approved design and your final content. Output: a working site on staging, and a draft handover document. Owner: dadmor.
Launch and handover. Input: the site you approved. Output: the live site, a walkthrough, and the final handover document. Owner: dadmor; domain and hosting access: you.

blocks.html: Deliverables
What makes it bigger or smaller

items: What pushes the work from S to M to L: how many pages, which features (forms, search, more than one language), which integrations (payment, booking, a content management system), and whether your content is ready.
Bilingual isn't just translation. It's two sets of content and an RTL and LTR check on every page, so we scope it separately.
From you we need: text and images, logo and brand identity, domain and hosting access, and one named person who can approve things.
What usually slows a build down: content that isn't ready (the classic), feedback that arrives late, and access nobody can find on launch day.

blocks.html: Rough size, honestly

items: Band S, M or L, worked out with the estimator's rule table. The fixed price comes after we talk, in a written proposal.

blocks.html: Honestly, content readiness and a clear page list move this band more than anything technical. And a band isn't a price or a deadline. Both of those come after the scoping conversation, in writing.
The fine print

items: We don't promise a particular Google ranking. What we hand over is structure, speed and a site technically ready for search.
Writing your content isn't part of this service unless the scope says so. For that, look at Marketing and content.
Domain, hosting and third-party costs are yours, and every account stays in your name.
Third-party services, payment gateways and booking tools, can change after launch. Support beyond the handover period needs its own written agreement.
We're one small studio and we take on a limited number of projects at a time, so your start date depends on the room we have when you come to us.
